title: Which SOLID principle does this code violate?
summary: This is a live-code-reading skill, not a lookup. Name the smell in plain English first, then map it to a letter, then propose the fix.

slides.markdown:
This question hands you a snippet and asks you to diagnose it live — a different skill from reciting definitions. It tests whether you can read unfamiliar code under time pressure and pattern-match it to a real failure mode, not whether you've memorized the acronym.

The reliable order: name the smell you see first, in plain English, *then* attach the letter, *then* propose a fix. Naming the letter before the smell is how people confidently name the wrong violation.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying question: a snippet now, or one to imagine?
slides.markdown:
Ask **"are you going to show me code, or do you want me to imagine a typical example?"** before assuming. Some interviewers pull up a real snippet on a shared screen; others want you to narrate a hypothetical class from scratch.

The two modes need different pacing — reading real code rewards going slowly and pointing at specific lines; narrating a hypothetical rewards picking a concrete, recognizable shape fast so you don't ramble.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: smell, letter, fix
slides.markdown:
Three steps, always in this order. **Name the smell** you actually see — "this method changes behavior based on a type check" — in plain English, no acronym yet. **Map it to the letter** — a type-check branch that grows a case per new type is OCP. **Propose the fix** — extract each branch into its own class behind a common interface.

Cross-link: **[common code smells](common-code-smells)** is the reference list of smells this skeleton draws from.

```python
class Order:
    def calculate_total(self): ...
    def save_to_db(self): ...
    def send_confirmation_email(self): ...
    def print_invoice(self): ...
```
Smell: `Order` changes for pricing rules, schema changes, email templates, *and* invoice formatting — four unrelated reasons to touch the same class. Fix: extract `OrderPricer`, `OrderRepository`, `OrderMailer`, `InvoicePrinter`; `Order` holds only data and delegates.

```python
def discount_for(order_type):
    if order_type == "retail": return 0.05
    elif order_type == "wholesale": return 0.15
    elif order_type == "vip": return 0.25
    # a new case gets added here every time a new order type ships
```
Smell: this function must be edited for every new order type, and every call site risks forgetting a case. Fix: a `discount()` method on each order-type class, looked up polymorphically instead of branched on.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: it violates two principles at once — which do you fix first?
slides.markdown:
Fix the one that's actively costing the team, not the one that feels more "textbook." A god-class that also has an OCP-violating switch inside one of its methods: fix SRP first — splitting it isolates the switch into a smaller, safer surface to then fix for OCP.

Saying "I'd fix SRP first because it de-risks the OCP fix" reads far stronger than picking one arbitrarily.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: refactoring it live, in under two minutes
slides.markdown:
Don't attempt the full fix on the whiteboard — narrate the shape of it and write only the signatures. For the OCP switch: "I'd introduce an `OrderType` interface with a `discount()` method, one implementation per type, and a lookup table or factory replacing the `if/elif` chain" — then sketch just the interface and one implementation, not all five.

Interviewers are scoring the plan's shape, not full working code in two minutes.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: does it matter which letter it is, if you're unsure?
slides.markdown:
The fix matters more than the label. If you can describe the smell precisely and propose a sound fix, getting the exact letter slightly wrong (calling an OCP violation an SRP one, say) costs you little — most real violations blur boundaries anyway.

Saying "I'm not 100% sure if this is OCP or SRP, but here's the fix either way" is a stronger answer than freezing because you can't name the letter with certainty.

slides.sectionTitle: Weak answer: naming a principle with no specific line
slides.markdown:
**Weak belief:** saying "this violates SRP" and stopping there, without pointing at which lines or methods actually cause the problem.

**Why it's weak:** it's unfalsifiable — the interviewer can't tell if you actually saw the violation or guessed based on the question's framing.

**Correct model:** point at the specific method or branch, describe in one sentence why it's a separate reason to change, then name the letter.

slides.sectionTitle: Wrong answer: naming a violation that isn't there
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** confidently naming a violation to sound sharp, even when the code doesn't actually exhibit it — for example calling a clean, single-purpose `Order` class an SRP violation because it happens to have four methods.

**Why it's wrong:** method count isn't a responsibility signal, and a false-positive diagnosis reads worse than saying "I don't see an obvious violation here."

**Correct model:** it's fine, and stronger, to say a piece of code looks clean if it does.

"I read through the code and I'm going to name what I actually see, then attach the letter. This function branches on a type string and adds a case per new type — that's a change-every-time-you-extend smell, which is the OCP violation. The fix: give each order type its own class with a `discount()` method, and replace the branch with a lookup so adding a type means adding a class, not editing this function."

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: reading the code vs guessing from the question
slides.markdown:
Two very different habits candidates fall into under pressure:

| | Reads the code first | Guesses from the question's framing |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | Slightly slower to start | Fast, but often wrong |
| Accuracy | Names the actual smell present | Names whatever letter the question title hints at |
| Recovery if wrong | Easy — re-reads and corrects | Hard — has to backtrack a confident claim |

How to decide: always spend the first ten seconds reading, even under time pressure — guessing is the false economy here.
